newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Bre-X workers being "held" by colleagues - reports.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X workers being "held" by colleagues - reports.

text.p: Two senior Indonesian employees of Canadian exploration company Bre-X Minerals Ltd were being "held" by hundreds of their colleagues at the Busang base camp in East Kalimantan, according to news reports on Tuesday.

Bre-X's head of administration and personnel, identified by the official Antara news agency as Idris, and surveyor Agus Tripadi have reportedly been held by the workers since Sunday ahead of a proposed lay-off.
It quoted local military commander Aji Suryanata Kesuma, however, as saying he had yet to receive such information.
"It is not likely that they are being held as captives, but only so that the company will not fail to fulfill its obligations to workers who will be laid off," Kesuma said.

Military and police officials contacted in the East Kalimantan capital Samarinda and the Kutai regency, where the Busang property is located, said they had not received any reports of Bre-X employees being held hostage.
The afternoon Suara Pembaruan newspaper quoted Bre-X workers as saying the two men were being held because they were worried they would not be paid their wages and lay-off compensation.
Antara quoted a source as saying the workers' compensation could be as much as 1.5 billion rupiah (US$ 620,000).
The Busang discovery was touted by Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd as the largest gold find of the century, but independent tests showed it contained virtually no gold.
Indonesia has frozen all activites of Bre-X and its subsidiaries operating in the country until police investigations into the scandal are completed.
Newspapers have said many of the around 400 Bre-X employees at the Busang project could be fired because of the scandal.
Meanwhile, an officer from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) on Tuesday ended a four-day visit to Indonesia to discuss investigations into Busang.
Douglas Herda, senior RCMP liaison officer for Southeast Asia, declined to comment on the outcome of his trip, which came on the heels of the collapse of the Busang project.
"I cannot comment on anything. Any information will have to come from Canada," he told Reuters before leaving for Singapore, where he is based.
Suara Pembaruan reported on Tuesday that a Singapore-based Canadian police officer had visited Bre-X's warehouse in Samarinda, where the company's core samples were stored.
The newspaper quoted an unidentified employee at the warehouse as saying the officer and a local policeman checked documents at the warehouse. It did not identify Herda.
Consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd said in its audit report on Busang that Bre-X's storage warehouse in Samarinda was the most likely place for any tampering with core samples.
Brigadier-General Ahwil Luthan, secretary of the National Central Bureau that handles investigations requiring Interpol assistance, denied Herda had visited Samarinda.
"He was just in Jakarta," he told Reuters. "He didn't go there," he said, when asked to comment on the newspaper report.
The Busang project, in which the Indonesian government held a 10-percent stake, collapsed after Strathcona said it found no economic gold deposit on the property.
Strathcona also said the Bre-X data on the Busang discovery had been falsified on an unprecedented scale.
Indonesian and Canadian police are investigating the scandal -- the biggest mining fraud in history.
